title: Selective, durable control of pathological chronic pain

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a mechanism-specific treatment that durably controls pathological chronic pain while preserving protective nociception: the ability to detect potentially damaging events and respond to them. The intended benefit is relief substantial enough to improve daily life, sustained for as long as treatment is needed, without escalating doses, addiction, or disabling central-nervous-system effects. This is a target capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

The defining distinction is between suppressing an ongoing pathological pain state and retaining useful warning sensation. A treatment could relieve pain yet fall short if it also prevented patients from recognizing new injuries, lost effectiveness over time, or caused unacceptable impairment. Conversely, successful pain control would not necessarily repair the disease or tissue damage producing the pain. These distinctions define the proposed capability independently of any particular drug or delivery method.

Peripheral sodium-channel targeting provides a demonstrated component of pain treatment: the FDA documented acute postoperative pain relief with oral suzetrigine. That achievement establishes acute analgesic efficacy in the studied settings, but the supplied release does not demonstrate the combination of chronic relief, preserved protective sensation, and long-term tolerability required here.

significance.text: As a conditional clinical judgment, combining durable relief with preserved warning sensation would substantially change chronic pain treatment. The direct consequence would be control of spontaneous pain and its interference with daily life in patients for whom efficacy was demonstrated. Sustained benefit without dose escalation or disabling central effects would make continued treatment more useful, rather than merely producing a short period of analgesia.

Reduced opioid-related harm is a plausible downstream benefit to the extent that an effective treatment replaces opioid exposure. It is not an automatic consequence of introducing another analgesic: the effect would depend on prescribing, uptake, and actual substitution. The FDA release identifies an opportunity for a new non-opioid acute-pain treatment to mitigate some opioid-associated risks, but does not establish that outcome for durable chronic-pain treatment.

The scope of the proposed advance is pain control, not repair of an injured nerve, damaged joint, cancer, or other underlying cause. Improved activity or rehabilitation would be conditional downstream possibilities, not guaranteed restoration of tissue or function. The supplied evidence also does not substantiate broad claims that existing chronic-pain drugs generally provide only partial relief, impair thinking, cause dependence, or lose effectiveness; those comparisons require treatment-specific evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved capability within this record is selective, sustained control of pathological chronic pain in people. The supplied evidence demonstrates acute postoperative analgesia, but does not show that pathological chronic pain can be suppressed while protective nociception remains intact over continued treatment. This is a boundary of the supplied evidence, not proof that no intervention anywhere has achieved the capability.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: the central challenge is to identify and control a mechanism sustaining the pathological pain state with sufficient selectivity to spare useful warning signals. A mechanism-specific intervention must do more than engage a pain-related target: its effects must separate the unwanted persistent state from protective responses in patients. The supplied material does not establish that this separation is technically feasible, identify a validated mechanism that accomplishes it, or show how broadly such a mechanism would apply across chronic-pain conditions.

Further proposed barriers concern durability, safety, and measurement. Continued treatment must retain clinically meaningful benefit without requiring progressive dose increases, and must avoid unacceptable dependence, misuse, respiratory depression, or central impairment. Clinical evaluation must distinguish pain relief from sedation or reduced activity, assess protective sensation directly, and determine whether benefit extends beyond one selected condition. Acute efficacy alone cannot resolve these requirements.

current_state.text: On 30 January 2025, the FDA approved Journavx (suzetrigine) 50-milligram oral tablets, described as a first-in-class non-opioid analgesic, for moderate to severe acute pain in adults. The release describes targeting sodium channels in the peripheral nervous system. Although the earlier research identifies suzetrigine as a NaV1.8 inhibitor, the supplied FDA release does not identify the channel subtype, so that specificity is not treated as verified by this record.

Two randomized trials evaluated pain after abdominoplasty and after bunionectomy. Both showed statistically significant pain reduction compared with placebo. Participants whose pain control was inadequate could use ibuprofen as rescue medication. These findings support acute postoperative efficacy under the studied conditions; the supplied review does not establish a numerical effect size or superiority over existing non-opioid chronic-pain care.

FDA described safety data from 874 participants in the controlled surgical trials, with supportive data from 256 participants in an open-label study involving varied acute-pain conditions. These are safety-study participant counts, not evidence of long-term chronic-pain efficacy or of preserved protective nociception. The acute-pain indication and these studies do not establish freedom from tolerance, dependence, or other risks during prolonged treatment.

The supplied review reports that the FDA release was available in full, with no indicated truncation or extraction problems. Its retrieval on 1 November 2026 does not update its January 2025 content. No peer-reviewed chronic-pain trial, successor-treatment evidence, or documented search covering subsequent developments was supplied. The record therefore establishes the historical acute-pain advance but cannot determine the broader state of selective chronic-pain control as of November 2026. Missing evidence here does not show that later results are false or nonexistent.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: randomized trials in at least two common chronic-pain states, such as painful diabetic neuropathy and chronic neuropathic low-back or radicular pain, would show large, durable reductions in spontaneous pain and interference with daily life. Each trial would specify an appropriate existing non-opioid care comparator and demonstrate superiority on prespecified clinically meaningful outcomes. These are proposed criteria, not established authoritative standards; no particular pain-scale point reduction is adopted as a universal cutoff.
completion_criteria.label: Superior pain relief and functioning in two chronic-pain states

completion_criteria.text: Durability would require a prespecified follow-up period appropriate to continued chronic-pain treatment, together with reporting of dose changes, treatment discontinuation, and persistence of functional benefit. Protective nociception would need direct assessment rather than inference from pain scores alone. Relief confined to the first days after surgery would not satisfy the proposal. The supplied evidence does not justify a particular minimum duration or a specific protective-sensation testing protocol.
completion_criteria.label: Durable functional benefit and protective nociception are directly assessed

completion_criteria.text: Trials and subsequent follow-up would monitor tolerance, dependence, misuse, respiratory depression, disabling central effects, and clinically relevant consequences of impaired warning sensation. An absence of detected events would need interpretation against sample size, exposure duration, and ascertainment methods; it would not establish zero risk. Reproducible results across independent studies would strengthen the case, with transparent reporting of nonresponders, adverse effects, and populations excluded from testing.
completion_criteria.label: Safety risks are monitored and interpreted against trial exposure

completion_criteria.text: Success would establish the capability within the tested indications, patient groups, doses, and treatment durations. Two positive indications would demonstrate useful breadth across those conditions, not universal efficacy for all chronic pain. Practical boundaries would include whether patients can sustain treatment, whether benefit remains meaningful during ordinary daily activity, and whether underlying disease still requires separate treatment.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated capability stays within tested indications and treatment conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CLM-04, Restoration of adult human central nervous system circuitry after injury, overlaps through neural function and injury-related symptoms. Its defining goal is restoration of circuitry, whereas CLM-12 concerns selective control of pathological pain and could succeed without rebuilding damaged circuitry. CLM-03, Arrest and recovery of function in symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease, likewise targets disease arrest and functional recovery; a neurological treatment setting alone does not make it the same capability.

Roster-based synthesis: CLM-01, Programmable antigen-specific immune tolerance, and CLM-09, Curative in vivo genome writing beyond the liver, describe distinct biological capabilities that could conceivably contribute to a future pain intervention. That possibility is conceptual, not established by the supplied evidence. CLM-12 does not require immune tolerance or genome writing, and achieving either of those capabilities would not itself demonstrate selective, durable pain control.

Roster-based synthesis: CLM-07, Reproducible eradication of metastatic carcinoma, illustrates the distinction between controlling pain and removing its cause. Relief of cancer-related pain would not establish carcinoma eradication, while cancer eradication would require its own disease-specific evidence. Similarly, CLM-06, Therapeutic remuscularization of the adult human heart, and CLM-15, Restoration of nephron number in the adult human kidney, concern tissue restoration that pain relief alone cannot demonstrate.

Roster-based synthesis: CLM-08, Safe multi-tissue reversal of human biological aging, could share downstream goals involving function and quality of life, but has a different biological endpoint. Chronic-pain improvement would not by itself demonstrate reversal of aging. The remaining roster entries address infection clearance or prevention, transplantation and organ construction, cancer screening, or blood replacement; no specific mechanistic overlap with selective chronic-pain control is established in the supplied material.

unresolved_issues: No documented search covering subsequent developments was supplied, so the state of the broader capability through November 2026 remains undetermined.
The NaV1.8 subtype identification in the earlier research remains unverified by the supplied source; omission from this release is not evidence that the identification is false.
The supplied material does not establish a mechanism that separates pathological chronic pain from protective nociception in people or determine how broadly such selectivity could apply.

No supplied chronic-pain trial establishes sustained benefit, preserved protective sensation, or long-term avoidance of tolerance, dependence, misuse, respiratory depression, and disabling central effects.
Comparator regimens, clinically meaningful benefit thresholds, follow-up duration, protective-nociception measures, and safety-study size remain to be specified for the proposed demonstrations.
Broad claims about the shortcomings of existing chronic-pain treatments require additional treatment-specific evidence.
No substantive review recommendation was rejected; operational details that the review identified as necessary remain explicitly unresolved.

brief.title: Lasting pain relief that keeps injury warnings intact
possible: People with persistent pain could get lasting relief while still feeling the warning pain of a new injury. Treatment would target the process sustaining their pain, remain effective without rising doses, and avoid addiction or disabling effects on thinking and alertness.
why: Pain would interfere less with daily life, and continued treatment would keep helping people function. Preserving warning pain would let them recognize new injuries while controlling the pain that persists.

sources.showed: Suzetrigine reduced short-term pain after surgery compared with placebo, a dummy treatment. It targets sodium channels, proteins that help nerves carry pain signals outside the brain and spinal cord.
sources.quote: Both trials demonstrated a statistically significant superior reduction in pain with Journavx compared to placebo.
sources.cited_for: Targeting pain signals outside the brain can provide pain relief after surgery.
sources.not_established: Short-term surgical pain relief does not establish lasting chronic-pain control or preserved injury warnings.

sources.showed: An implanted device delivering electrical pulses to the spinal cord provided pain relief lasting 24 months in patients with diabetes-related nerve pain. Sleep and quality of life also improved.
sources.quote: Furthermore, the majority of participants demonstrated neurological improvement.
sources.cited_for: Spinal cord stimulation can provide sustained relief in a selected chronic-pain condition.
sources.not_established: Improved nerve examinations do not establish that patients reliably retain injury-warning pain during everyday life.

sources.showed: An earlier report from the same trial found better pain relief with spinal cord stimulation plus usual care than with usual care alone. Patients knew which treatment they received.
sources.quote: there was a significant benefit of 10-kHz spinal cord stimulation
sources.cited_for: The trial supports pain relief without worsening existing nerve problems in diabetes-related nerve pain.
sources.not_established: This report does not establish lasting selective pain control across different chronic-pain conditions.

sources.showed: A conference abstract reported reduced diabetes-related nerve pain during 12 weeks of suzetrigine treatment. It reported no serious adverse events, meaning medical problems during treatment, linked to the drug.
sources.quote: there were no serious AEs related to suzetrigine.
sources.cited_for: Suzetrigine has shown an early clinical signal of benefit for chronic nerve pain.
sources.not_established: The abstract does not establish superiority over existing care, preserved warning sensation, or long-term safety.

shown: Petersen and colleagues reported the longest-lasting chronic-pain benefit among these studies: spinal cord stimulation relieved diabetes-related nerve pain for 24 months, with improved sleep and nerve examinations. Patients knew their treatment, and the longer follow-up included people who switched from usual care.

Suzetrigine has demonstrated pain relief after surgery and early benefit in diabetes-related nerve pain. Neither approach yet establishes the full combination of lasting chronic-pain relief, preserved injury warnings, and acceptable long-term risks.
missing: Trials must establish substantial, lasting pain relief and better daily functioning across different chronic-pain conditions.
Direct testing must establish that patients retain useful injury-warning pain during continued treatment.
Long-term follow-up must establish sustained benefit without rising doses, addiction, or disabling effects on alertness.

milestones.label: Better pain relief and functioning in two chronic-pain conditions
milestones.explanation: Randomized trials in two common chronic-pain conditions would have to beat appropriate existing non-opioid care on meaningful pain relief and daily functioning. This would establish useful benefit across conditions.

milestones.label: Lasting daily benefit with injury warnings preserved
milestones.explanation: Follow-up would have to track lasting functional benefit, dose changes, treatment stopping, and direct tests of injury-warning sensation. This would distinguish sustained selective relief from temporary pain suppression.

milestones.label: Safety risks measured over continued treatment
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to monitor fading benefit, dependence, misuse, slowed breathing, disabling brain effects, and harm from missed warnings. Their size and duration would determine how much reassurance absent events provide.

milestones.label: Useful treatment within clearly tested limits
milestones.explanation: Results would have to establish benefit during ordinary activity within tested conditions, patient groups, doses, and durations. This would define who can sustain useful treatment while underlying disease receives separate care.

uncertain: Can treatment separate persistent pathological pain from useful injury warnings, and how widely could that separation work?
What benefit threshold, follow-up period, and warning-sensation tests would adequately demonstrate success?
How much treatment exposure would reveal uncommon harms and loss of effectiveness?

page.title: Chronic pain relief with preserved protective nociception
page.definition: A treatment targeting a defined pain mechanism controls pain persisting or recurring for more than 3 months while preserving nociception, the neural encoding of potentially damaging stimuli, and injury avoidance. Relief and improved function persist during continued treatment without progressive dose increases, addiction, dependence or disabling impairment.

goal.need: In the 2023 US National Health Interview Survey, 34.9% of adults reporting chronic pain also had pain that limited life or work on most days or every day. This makes activity limitation an outcome alongside pain intensity. The table gives prevalence among all adults.

figures.caption: Chronic pain among US adults in 2023
figures.note: Adults aged 18 years and older in the civilian noninstitutionalized population. Chronic pain means pain on most days or every day during the preceding 3 months; high-impact chronic pain additionally limits life or work that frequently.

completion.title: A treatment controls chronic pain for at least 6 months while preserving protective nociception.
completion.criterion: For one specified chronic-pain indication, controlled human evidence establishes maintained pain relief and functional improvement after at least 6 months, together with retained injury-warning sensation and avoidance responses on direct tests during treatment. Benefit persists at a maintained dose without addiction, clinically important dependence or disabling impairment. The prospective protocol must specify sensory preservation margins, efficacy endpoints, harm limits and follow-up. This provisional composite has no externally endorsed sensory preservation margin.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional synthesis because no outside body located defines the combined capability.
completion.basis: FDA and EMA analgesic-development guidance, ICH E1, NIH HEAL priorities, IASP terminology and IMMPACT recommendations were searched for a joint durability and protective-nociception test; none was found. The six-month component follows EMA's maintenance-of-efficacy design. Sensory preservation remains a proposed requirement without a published universal pass/fail margin.

milestones.title: A pain-treatment candidate shows target-linked biological activity in laboratory systems and living animals.
milestones.criterion: NIH HEAL Development-stage entry requires an identified candidate, evidence connecting its target to the pain indication, biological activity in vitro and in vivo, and absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity properties appropriate for clinical use. It specifies no universal numerical cutoff. Component evidence: suzetrigine inhibited action-potential firing in 10 of 17 sensory neurons from 3 human donors at concentrations ≥1 nM. This demonstrates cellular pharmacology, not preservation of protective nociception.
milestones.set_by: NIH HEAL Initiative, RFA-NS-21-010, General Entry Criteria; these criteria concern small molecules and biologics.
milestones.threshold_quote: the proposed therapeutic must have in vitro and in vivo biological activity and ADMET properties appropriate for the intended clinical use.

milestones.title: A pain-treatment candidate reaches human dosing with exposure and acute safety characterization.
milestones.criterion: A phase 1 study administers the candidate to people and characterizes human exposure, dose tolerance and acute adverse effects. FDA defines this stage without a universal sample-size or toxicity cutoff. Its suzetrigine review lists VX19-548-001: 40 healthy adults in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study using single oral doses of 7.5–65 mg. This establishes human dosing, not chronic-pain efficacy.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Step 3: Clinical Research, description of phase 1 drug studies.
milestones.threshold_quote: how much of a drug the body can tolerate and what its acute side effects are.

milestones.title: A chronic-pain treatment reduces mean pain from baseline at 12 weeks in a phase 2 study.
milestones.criterion: Protocol VX21-548-103 tests within-group change in weekly mean daily pain on a 0–10 scale at 12 weeks. Its 2025 abstract reports 192 adults; suzetrigine 69 mg/day reduced pain by 2.26 points (95% CI, 1.70–2.82), without a placebo arm. In lumbosacral radiculopathy, 218 enrolled participants yielded changes of −2.02 with suzetrigine (n=102) and −1.98 with placebo (n=100). These reports are not peer reviewed and establish no superiority over control. On 2 November 2026, Vertex listed two ongoing phase 3 diabetic-neuropathy studies.
milestones.set_by: Vertex Pharmaceuticals, protocol VX21-548-103, version 3.0, dated 17 February 2023, registered as NCT05660538; this endpoint was written for painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary analysis will be a within-group comparison in any VX-548 dose group.

milestones.title: A chronic-pain treatment gives ≥50% relief without neurological worsening at 3 months.
milestones.criterion: The SENZA-PDN primary endpoint combines ≥50% pain reduction on a 0–10 cm visual analogue scale with no meaningful worsening of baseline neurological deficits at 3 months; groups are compared with a two-sided significance level of 0.05. Among 216 randomized adults with painful diabetic neuropathy, 75/95 evaluable participants receiving 10 kHz spinal cord stimulation plus conventional medical management met it, versus 5/94 receiving medical management alone (P<0.001). Treatment was unblinded. This endpoint does not establish preserved protective nociception.
milestones.set_by: Nevro and SENZA-PDN investigators, prespecified primary endpoint of NCT03228420, reproduced in the primary publication; written for painful diabetic neuropathy.
milestones.threshold_quote: participants with 50% pain relief or more on VAS without worsening of baseline neurological deficits at 3 months.

milestones.title: A chronic-pain drug has 100 patients treated for 1 year and 300–600 treated for 6 months.
milestones.criterion: For drugs intended for treatment longer than 6 months, ICH E1 generally anticipates about 1,500 exposed people overall, 300–600 patients treated for 6 months, and 100 for at least 1 year at intended clinical doses; exceptions require individualized assessment. Exposure alone does not establish safety. FDA approved suzetrigine for acute pain on 30 January 2025; its release describes 874 controlled-study safety recipients and 256 open-label recipients, without establishing these long-term exposures.
milestones.set_by: International Conference on Harmonisation, E1, paragraphs 4–7; a drug-specific exposure benchmark for long-term treatment of non-life-threatening conditions.
milestones.threshold_quote: 100 patients exposed for a minimum of one-year is considered to be acceptable to include as part of the safety data base.

milestones.title: A chronic-pain treatment retains efficacy after at least 6 months of stable treatment.
milestones.criterion: EMA's drug-specific design tests symptom relapse after randomization to continued treatment or placebo following ≥6 months of stable open-label treatment; time to relapse or relapse proportion establishes maintenance. Other justified designs are allowed, and tolerance must be characterized. Related device evidence: at 24 months, 128/142 implanted SENZA-PDN participants had ≥50% pain relief and 92/140 had neurological improvement; 5/154 implants were removed for infection. Follow-up included 58 crossovers, lacked an untreated control, and used an unvalidated, unblinded neurological examination. It did not establish retained injury-warning pain.
milestones.set_by: EMA Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, analgesic-development guideline, section 5.2.5; this is a drug-specific maintenance-of-efficacy design.
milestones.threshold_quote: Following stable open label treatment for at least 6 months, patients are randomised to receive either active or placebo.

not_found: No outside document located defined a combined completion test for maintained chronic-pain relief, preserved protective nociception, dose stability and freedom from clinically important dependence or impairment.
No externally endorsed clinical margin for preservation of injury-warning sensation during continued chronic-pain treatment was located.
ClinicalTrials.gov study pages returned no readable study details; the diabetic-neuropathy phase 2 protocol was accessible separately.
